title: Indra goes back
hook: Indra and Virochana look into the water for the self, and only Indra goes back
carry: viveka: telling the self from what it sees
tomorrow: The serpent who came to teach

segments.voice: Yesterday: apavarga, and your line, bhoga and apavarga: the world is there for both, experience and freedom. Today, a king of the gods who wouldn't stop at the first answer.
screen: `BHOGA AND APAVARGA: THE WORLD IS FOR BOTH — EXPERIENCE AND FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Two students arrive at a teacher's door with firewood in their hands, the old sign of asking to learn. One is Indra, king of the gods. The other is Virochana, king of the demons. Both have heard the teacher, Prajapati, speak of a self that never ages, never dies, never grieves, and both want it. For thirty-two years they live with him and wait. Then Prajapati tells them to put on their finest clothes and look into a pan of water. That, he says, is the self. Both walk away happy. Only one of them comes back.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE TEACHER.` → `LOOK INTO THE WATER.` → `ONLY ONE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Chandogya Upanishad. Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self: dress it, feed it, serve it. Indra gets partway home and stops. If the body is dressed up, the reflection is dressed up. If the body is hurt, the reflection is hurt. If the body dies, this self dies too. That can't be the deathless one. So he goes back. Thirty-two more years, and a new answer: the one who dreams. Again he doubts, and goes back. Thirty-two more, and another answer. He goes back once more. A hundred and one years in all, before Prajapati tells him plainly: the body is mortal, a home for the self, which has no body at all. Hindus call that self the atman. You can hear this week's book in that story. Patanjali names the remedy for suffering in sutra 2.26: viveka, discernment, telling the seer from the seen, the self from everything it looks at, including the body and the mind. And he adds one word: aviplava, unwavering. Virochana had a flash and stopped. Indra kept going until the seeing held. Sutra 2.28 says how it grows: practice the limbs of yoga, and as impurity dwindles, the light of knowledge shines all the way to discernment. Day to day, viveka sounds small: this is a mood, not me. This is a thought, not the one watching it. Said once, it's a flash. Said every day, it's Indra going back.
screen: `VIROCHANA STOPS AT THE REFLECTION.` · `INDRA GOES BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VIVEKA — TELLING APART.` · `AVIPLAVA — UNWAVERING.` · then, large: `VIVEKA.`

segments.voice: Count the out-breaths from one to ten, then start again; if you keep a mala, move one bead with each breath instead. When a thought pulls you off count, notice it plainly, a thought, not the one watching it, and go back to one. Losing count isn't failure: noticing is the discernment, and coming back, again and again, like Indra, is the steadiness.
Aviplava. Unwavering discernment between seer and seen, held so steady it stops wavering.
Your line: viveka, telling the self from what it sees. Virochana stopped at the reflection; Indra kept going back. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 456 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SERPENT WHO CAME TO TEACH.`

howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, discernment between awareness and what it is aware of is the central means of liberation, cultivated over years through study, the ethical disciplines and meditation, usually under a teacher's guidance.

guess: a sudden flash of insight on a mountain
a calm that comes from ignoring thoughts

match.prompt: two students and a remedy — tap the pairs.
pairs: took the reflection for the self
went back until the seeing held
telling the seer from the seen

myth: at first, Indra and Virochana both went away happy
both took the reflection in the water for the self; only Indra saw the problem on the way home.
for Patanjali, one flash of insight is enough
2.26 asks for discernment that is unwavering, aviplava.
the limbs of yoga make the light of knowledge shine brighter
2.28: as impurity dwindles, the light shines all the way to discernment.

fork.setup: after one deep evening you felt sure: you are not your moods. by Monday it's gone. which student fits Patanjali's remedy?
options: Virochana: the first answer felt good, so keep it.
Indra: go back and keep practicing until it holds.
neither: the evening must have been fake.
fork.reveal: Indra went back for a hundred and one years in all; 2.26 asks for discernment that is aviplava, unwavering, and 2.28 says the limbs of yoga grow it.

original.note: Sanskrit viveka: discernment, discrimination, telling one thing from another; in 2.26, viveka-khyāti.

trapdoor: what you thought: discernment means good taste or careful judgment.
what it means: telling the self from everything it sees, body and mind included, held so steadily it never wavers.

what a scholar hears: viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah (2.26); the Chandogya's Indra, who returns to Prajapati three times, is the classic picture of discernment that won't settle for the reflection.
recall: one-pointed: a mind on a single object

chat.meaning: Indra went back to his teacher again and again until he could tell the self from the body. Patanjali asks for discernment that is unwavering, and says it grows with practice.

tie.story: Indra took his reflection for the self, saw the problem, and went back to Prajapati until the seeing held.
tie.friend: Priya's calm after class wasn't fake; like Indra, she keeps coming back until it stops wavering.
tie.you: what clear moment of yours needs a second visit?

viveka.meaning: discernment: telling one thing from another

Virochana.meaning: king of the demons, who stopped at the reflection

Prajapati.meaning: the creator, teacher of Indra and Virochana

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.12 (Indra and Virochana with Prajapati; the reflection in water; Indra's returns, 101 years in all)
Yoga Sutra 2.26 (unwavering discriminative discernment is the means of removal)
Yoga Sutra 2.28 (the limbs of yoga and the light of knowledge)

notes: Sanskrit of 2.26 given as viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah; confirm.
The sooty lamp-glass image is the script's illustration, not a quotation from the commentary.
The seven stages of 2.27 are listed in the Yoga Bhashya; not named in the script to keep one idea.
